title: Nothing better than trust in God
source_text: Μὴ ὑπολάβῃς δέ με οὐχ ἁρμοζόντως τῷ Χριστιανῶν λόγῳ παρειληφέναι πρὸς τὸν Κέλσον τοὺς περὶ τῆς ἀθανασίας ἢ τῆς ἐπιδιαμονῆς τῆς ψυχῆς φιλοσοφήσαντας· πρὸς οὓς κοινά τινα ἔχοντες εὐκαιρότερον παραστήσομεν ὅτι ἡ μέλλουσα μακαρία ζωὴ μόνοις ἔσται τοῖς (τὴν) κατὰ τὸν Ἰησοῦν θεοσέβειαν καὶ εἰς τὸν τῶν ὅλων δημιουργὸν εὐσέβειαν εἰλικρινῆ καὶ καθαρὰν καὶ ἄμικτον πρὸς ὅτι ποτ᾿ οὖν γενητὸν παραδεξαμένοις. ποίων δὲ κρειττόνων καταφρονεῖν παραπείθομεν τοὺς ἀνθρώπους, παραδεικνύτω ὁ βουλόμενος· καὶ ἀντιπαραθέτω τὸ καθ᾿ ἡμᾶς παρὰ θεῷ ἐν Χριστῷ, τουτέστι τῷ λόγῳ καὶ τῆ σοφίᾳ καὶ πάσῃ ἀρετῇ. τέλος μακάριον τοῖς ἀμέμπτως καὶ καθαρῶς βιώσασι καὶ τὴν πρὸς τὸν τῶν ὅλων θεὸν ἀγάπην ἀδιαίρετον καὶ ἄσχιστον ἀνειληφόσι συμβησόμενον, καὶ δωρεᾷ θεοῦ ἀπαντησόμενον. τῷ καθ᾿ ἑκάστην φιλόσοφον αἵρεσιν ἐν Ἕλλησιν ἢ βαρβάροις ἢ μυστηριώδη ἐπαγγελίαν τέλει· καὶ δεικνύτω τὸ κατά τινα τῶν ἄλλων τέλος κρεῖττον τοῦ καθ᾿ ἡμᾶς καὶ ἀκόλουθον μὲν ὡς ἀληθὲς ἐκεῖνο τὸ δ᾿ ἡμέτερον οὐχ ἁρμόζον δωρεᾷ θεοῦ οὐδὲ τοῖς εὖ βιώσασιν. ἢ οὐχ ὑπὸ θείου πνεύματος. πληρώσαντος τὰς τῶν καθαρῶν προφητῶν ψυχὰς. ταῦτα λελέχθαι. δεικνύτω δ᾿ ὁ βουλόμενος κρείττονας τοὺς ὁμολογουμένους παρὰ πᾶσιν ἀνθρωπίνους λόγους τῶν ἀποδεικνυμένων θείων καὶ ἐκ θεοφορίας ἀπηγγελμένων. τίνων δὲ καὶ κρειττόνων τοὺς ἀποδεχομένους διδάσκομεν ἄμεινον ἀπαλλάξειν; εἰ γὰρ μὴ φορτικὸν εἰπεῖν, αὐτόθεν φαίνεται ὅτι οὐδὲν οὐκ ἐπινοηθῆναι ὡς κρεῖττον εἶναι δύναται τοῦ ἐμπιστεῦσαι ἑαυτὸν τῷ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεῷ καὶ ἀναθεῖναι διδασκαλίᾳ, παντὸς μὲν ἀφιστάσῃ γενητοῦ προσαγούσῃ δὲ δι᾿ ἐμψύχου καὶ ζῶντος λόγου, ὅς ἐστι καὶ σοφία ζῶσα καὶ υἱὸς θεοῦ, τῷ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεῷ. ἀλλὰ γὰρ αὐτάρκη περιγραφὴν ἐν τούτοις καὶ τοῦ τρίτου τόμου τῶν πρὸς τὸ Κέλσου σύγγραμμα ἡμῖν ὑπαγορευθέντων εἰληφότος, αὐτοῦ που καταπαύσομεν τὸν λόγον, ἐν τοῖς ἑξῆς πρὸς τὰ μετὰ τοῦτο γεγραμμένα τῷ Κέλσῳ ἀγωνιούμενοι.
pass_a_gloss: Do not suppose (ὑπολαμβάνω) that I have not fittingly (οὐχ ἁρμοζόντως) for the Christians' word brought in (παραλαμβάνω) against Celsus those who philosophised about immortality (ἀθανασία) or survival (ἐπιδιαμονή) of the soul; with whom having some things in common (κοινά) we shall more opportunely (εὐκαιρότερον) show (παρίστημι) that the coming blessed life (ἡ μέλλουσα μακαρία ζωή) will be only for those who have accepted the worship of God (θεοσέβεια) according to Jesus and piety (εὐσέβεια) toward the Creator (δημιουργός) of the universe, sincere (εἰλικρινής), pure (καθαρά), and unmixed (ἄμικτος) with whatever is created (γενητόν). What better things (κρείττονα) we persuade people to despise, let whoever wishes demonstrate; and let him set over against (ἀντιπαρατίθημι) — the blessed end (τέλος μακάριον) according to us with God in Christ, that is, in the Word (λόγος) and the Wisdom (σοφία) and all virtue (ἀρετή), going to happen to those who lived blamelessly (ἀμέμπτως) and purely and took up undivided (ἀδιαίρετος) and unsplit (ἄσχιστος) love (ἀγάπη) for the God of the universe, and going to meet them by gift of God (δωρεᾷ θεοῦ) — the end according to each philosophical school (αἵρεσις) among Greeks or barbarians, or mysterious promise (μυστηριώδης ἐπαγγελία); and let him show the end according to one of the others better than ours, and that one consistent (ἀκόλουθον) as true, but ours not fitting a gift of God nor those who lived well; or that these were not said by a divine Spirit (θεῖον πνεῦμα) filling the souls of the pure prophets (προφῆται). Let whoever wishes show the words (λόγοι) agreed by all to be human better than those demonstrated (ἀποδείκνυμι) divine and announced from divine inspiration (θεοφορία). And from what better things do we teach those accepting that they will fare better being rid (ἄμεινον ἀπαλλάξειν)? For if it is not burdensome (φορτικόν) to say, it appears at once that nothing can be conceived as better than to entrust (ἐμπιστεύω) oneself to the God over all and devote (ἀνατίθημι) oneself to a teaching withdrawing (ἀφίστημι) from all created and bringing (προσάγω) through the ensouled (ἔμψυχος) and living (ζῶν) Word, who is also living Wisdom and Son of God (υἱὸς θεοῦ), to the God over all. But since the third volume (τόμος) of what was dictated (ὑπαγορεύω) by us against Celsus's treatise (σύγγραμμα) has taken a sufficient compass (αὐτάρκης περιγραφή) in these, here we shall stop (καταπαύω) the discourse, in what follows going to contend (ἀγωνίζομαι) against what was written after this by Celsus.
pass_b_english: Do not suppose that, in a way unfitting for the Christian doctrine, I have brought in against Celsus those who have taught philosophy on the immortality or the survival of the soul. Since we share some things with them, we shall find it easier to show that the blessed life to come will belong only to those who have accepted the worship of God that Jesus teaches, and a devotion to the Creator of the universe that is sincere and pure and unmixed with anything at all that is created.

Let anyone who wishes show which better things we persuade people to despise. Let him set against one another, on the one side, the blessed end that we teach, an end with God in Christ, that is, in the Word and Wisdom (1 Corinthians 1:24, 30) and all virtue, which will come to those who have lived blamelessly and purely and have taken up an undivided and unbroken love for the God of the universe, and will meet them as the gift of God; and on the other side, the end set forth by each philosophical school among Greeks or barbarians, or promised by a mystery. Let him show that the end held by one of the others is better than ours, and that it holds together as true, while ours befits neither the gift of God nor those who have lived well; or that these things were not spoken by the divine Spirit who filled the souls of the pure prophets. Let anyone who wishes show that words admitted by all to be human are better than words shown to be divine and proclaimed by divine inspiration.

And what better things do we teach those who accept our word that they will do better to be rid of? If it is not too bold to say so, it is plain at once that nothing can be conceived as better than to entrust oneself to the God who is over all, and to give oneself to a teaching that draws a person away from everything created and brings him, through the Word, who is animate and living, who is also living Wisdom and the Son of God, to the God who is over all.

But since the third book of what we have dictated against the treatise of Celsus has now reached a sufficient length with these words, we shall bring our discourse to a close here, and in the books that follow we shall contend against what Celsus wrote next.

choices.choice: Copy-text: staged source_3.json section 81 (Koetschau 3.81), the end of Book 3. '(τὴν)' is an editorial supplement. The long sentence 'ἀντιπαραθέτω τὸ καθ᾿ ἡμᾶς ... τέλος μακάριον ... τῷ καθ᾿ ἑκάστην φιλόσοφον αἵρεσιν ... τέλει' sets our end against (dative) the end of each school; the staged full stops inside it are punctuation noise, and the English keeps the comparison as 'on the one side ... on the other side'. 'ἐν Χριστῷ, τουτέστι τῷ λόγῳ καὶ τῇ σοφίᾳ καὶ πάσῃ ἀρετῇ' alludes to Christ as the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24) and to 1 Corinthians 1:30 (ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ, ὃς ἐγενήθη σοφία ἡμῖν ἀπὸ θεοῦ, with righteousness and sanctification, matching 'Wisdom and all virtue'); both cited inline. Possible but uncited allusions: 'δωρεᾷ θεοῦ' (Romans 6:23 uses χάρισμα; Ephesians 2:8 uses δῶρον); 'ζῶντος λόγου' (Hebrews 4:12); 'undivided love' for God (Matthew 22:37). 'θεῖον πνεῦμα' filling the prophets is the Holy Spirit, so 'the divine Spirit' is capitalised. 'ἔμψυχος' (having soul, animate) rendered 'animate', set against the lifeless idols of 3.76. 'εἰ μὴ φορτικὸν εἰπεῖν' rendered 'if it is not too bold to say so'. 'οὐδὲν οὐκ ἐπινοηθῆναι ... δύναται' would strictly give a cancelling double negative ('there is nothing that cannot be conceived'), which contradicts the argument; read by sense as 'nothing can be conceived as better' (perhaps οὐδ᾿ for οὐκ). 'μυστηριώδη ἐπαγγελίαν' read with 'τέλει' as 'the end ... promised by a mystery'.
'the blessed end that awaits us' changed to 'the blessed end that we teach' (τὸ καθ᾿ ἡμᾶς = the end in our teaching; 'awaits us' added a claim the Greek does not make)

Added 1 Corinthians 1:30 to the citation and bible_refs: 'ἐν Χριστῷ ... σοφίᾳ καὶ πάσῃ ἀρετῇ' matches 1:30 (in Christ Jesus, who became wisdom for us, and righteousness, sanctification) more closely than 1:24 alone, which names power and wisdom

'and that it is coherent, being true, while ours does not befit the gift of God, nor those who have lived well' smoothed to 'and that it holds together as true, while ours befits neither the gift of God nor those who have lived well' (same sense, less stiff order)
'living Wisdom and Son of God' given the article: 'living Wisdom and the Son of God'
Noted the 'οὐδὲν οὐκ' double negative in translator_notes; rendering by sense kept
Checked: Celsus's charge ('better things', 'better for them') answered word for word; Holy Spirit and Word capitals correct; closing sentence complete
